The calculator above groups spending into three buckets. Needs are costs you can't skip — housing, utilities, groceries, transportation, insurance, and the minimum payments on your debts. Wants are lifestyle choices like dining out, subscriptions, travel, and — often overlooked — an annual-fee credit card whose perks you don't actually use . Savings covers your emergency fund, retirement and investing, and any extra debt payoff above the minimum. The 50/30/20 rule, popularized by Senator Elizabeth Warren in her book All Your Worth, recommends 50% of after-tax income for needs, 30% for wants, and 20% for savings and debt. These are guidelines, not laws — in high-cost areas, needs often run higher, which simply means a smaller wants bucket. The zero-based method, used by Dave Ramsey's EveryDollar and others, takes a different angle: income minus expenses should equal zero, so every dollar is assigned a job before the month begins. Use the toggle above to switch between the two. To turn your leftover into wealth, see how to grow your savings and track your net worth . How to make a budget in 5 steps. First, tally your monthly take-home pay — the amount that actually hits your bank account after taxes and payroll deductions. Second, list every expense, splitting fixed costs (rent, insurance, loan payments) from variable ones (groceries, gas, dining). Third, pick a framework: the 50/30/20 rule if you want a quick guardrail, zero-based if you want tight control, or a household budget approach if two incomes fund one plan. Fourth, allocate leftover income to savings and debt payoff before wants — the CFPB's Money Smart guide calls this "paying yourself first." Fifth, review once a month and adjust; a budget only works if it survives contact with real spending. How to create a family budget adds three layers. Child care and education are often the second-largest line after housing — the BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey shows families with children spend 5–15% of income here, so treat it as a need, not a want. Joint accounts simplify the math but require a monthly money check-in so no one is surprised. Build a "kid inflation" buffer for growth spurts, school fees, and activities that arrive in lumpy bursts. The monthly budget calculator handles single-earner households; the household budget calculator is built for two incomes and shared bills. A looser cousin of 50/30/20 worth knowing is the 70/20/10 rule: 70% of income for everyday living expenses, 20% for savings, and 10% for debt payoff or giving. The appeal is simplicity — only three numbers instead of the finer needs/wants split 50/30/20 requires. The trade-off is real: lumping needs and wants into one 70% bucket makes it harder to spot which part of that spending is optional, so a household that could easily cut wants to escape high-interest debt may not notice the room to do it. 70/20/10 tends to fit best for disciplined savers with modest fixed costs and little or no high-interest debt; it fits worst for anyone carrying credit card balances, since the plan has no built-in signal to prioritize debt payoff the way 50/30/20's separate wants bucket does. If your fixed costs are unusually low relative to income, run both frameworks through the calculator above and see which produces a savings target you'll actually hit. Frequently asked questions What is a budget calculator? A budget calculator totals your take-home income and planned spending to show whether you have a surplus or a shortfall, and how your spending compares to recommended targets. The calculator above splits your money into needs, wants, and savings using the 50/30/20 rule, or lets you budget every dollar to zero. What is the 50/30/20 budget rule? The 50/30/20 rule allocates 50% of your after-tax income to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings and debt payoff. It comes from Senator Elizabeth Warren's book All Your Worth and is the most widely used quick-start budgeting framework because it needs just one number — your monthly take-home pay. What is the 70/20/10 budget rule and how does it compare to 50/30/20? The 70/20/10 rule allocates 70% of income to everyday living expenses, 20% to savings, and 10% to debt payoff or giving — one broad spending bucket instead of 50/30/20's separate needs and wants categories. It's simpler to set up, but because needs and wants are combined, it's harder to tell how much of that 70% is actually optional, which can hide room to cut spending and pay down debt faster. Is the 70/20/10 budget a good idea if I have credit card debt? Usually not as a starting point. Because 70/20/10 lumps needs and wants together and only sets aside 10% for debt, it doesn't force the same scrutiny of discretionary spending that 50/30/20's separate wants bucket does — and high-interest debt can grow faster than a flat 10% allocation pays it down. The 50/30/20 rule or a zero-based budget generally works better once you're actively paying off debt; see what credit score you'd need for a 0% APR balance transfer card as a faster way to attack the balance. Should I use gross or take-home income for a budget? Use take-home (after-tax) income — the amount that actually lands in your account. The 50/30/20 rule is built on after-tax pay. If you save for retirement through payroll deductions, you can add that back in and count it inside your 20% savings bucket. What is zero-based budgeting? Zero-based budgeting assigns every dollar of income a specific job until income minus expenses equals zero. It doesn't mean spending everything — money sent to savings or debt counts as a job. This is the method behind Dave Ramsey's EveryDollar app, and you can switch to it with the toggle in the calculator above. Do minimum debt payments count as a need or savings? Minimum required debt payments are needs — they're non-negotiable, so they belong in the 50% bucket. Any extra you pay above the minimum to get out of debt faster counts in the 20% savings and debt-payoff bucket. Keeping the two separate is the most common 50/30/20 mistake. If credit card debt is the target, see what credit score a 0% APR card typically needs before assuming a balance transfer is an option. How much of my income should I save? The 50/30/20 rule targets 20% of take-home pay for savings and debt payoff combined. If you have high-interest debt, focus that 20% on eliminating it first, then redirect it to an emergency fund and investing. See the savings goal calculator to plan a target, or read how to use a financial planning calculator to see how your savings rate connects to net worth and retirement readiness. Can selling unused PTO help me hit a savings goal faster? It can, if your employer offers a leave sell-back or PTO buyback option. Use the PTO cash-out calculator to see the gross and estimated net payout from selling a specific number of days, then route that lump sum straight into the savings or debt-payoff bucket above. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) describes the credit this way. Revenue Procedure 2026-26 sets the 2027 percentages used for the contribution. The calculator runs five steps: Divide expected 2027 household MAGI by the 2026 federal poverty level (FPL) for your household size. Find that percentage of FPL in the 2027 table below, and interpolate in a straight line inside its band. Multiply MAGI by the applicable percentage, then divide by 12 for the monthly contribution. Subtract the monthly contribution from the monthly benchmark premium. A negative result counts as zero. Cap the result at the monthly premium of the plan you choose. Written as one line, the credit is the smaller of two numbers: your plan premium, or the benchmark minus your contribution (never below zero). At 231.05% of FPL, income sits 31.05 points into the 50-point band from 200% to 250%. The rate climbs the same share of the way from 6.78% to 8.66%, which lands at about 7.95%. The calculator keeps the dollar result hidden until you confirm the nonfinancial conditions listed under When the ACA Subsidy Calculator Does Not Apply. Below 100% or above 400% of FPL, it shows an explanation in place of a credit. It estimates the federal credit only, with no state subsidy and no estimate of discounts on your share of costs for covered services. Income for the 2027 ACA Subsidy Calculator Enter your household's expected MAGI for 2027, the full year you want coverage. HealthCare.gov states that Marketplace savings are based on expected household income for the coverage year. Last year's income is only a starting point: the HealthCare.gov glossary says to begin with your most recent adjusted gross income (AGI) and adjust it for expected changes. MAGI does not appear as a line on your tax return. Build it in two steps: Start with AGI, which is line 11 of IRS Form 1040 . Add untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits, and tax-exempt interest. Leave out Supplemental Security Income (SSI). For many people, MAGI equals AGI or comes close. Take-home pay alone is the wrong input for this calculator. If your pay stub lists federal taxable wages, use that number. If it does not, HealthCare.gov says to start from gross income and subtract what your employer takes out for child care, health coverage, and retirement plans. Self-employment income goes in after business expenses. Some money stays out of the estimate entirely: child support gifts loan proceeds, such as student loans or home equity loans SSI veterans' disability payments workers' compensation Household size and household income follow tax rules. Your family for the credit is you, your spouse if you file jointly, and everyone you claim as a dependent, including dependents who do not need coverage. Household income adds the MAGI of each family member who is required to file a federal return, so a teenager's summer-job pay counts only if that teen must file. The coverage family is a smaller group. The IRS defines it as the family members enrolled through the Marketplace who cannot get Medicaid , Medicare, or affordable employer coverage. Enter the full tax household size and income, and use a benchmark premium that applies to the coverage family. ACA Subsidy Income Limits for 2027 For 2027 coverage, the ordinary federal premium tax credit range is household income from 100% to 400% of the 2026 federal poverty level for your household size. The IRS bases each year's credit on the poverty guidelines most recently published when open enrollment begins, so the 2025 credit used 2024 figures and the 2027 credit uses 2026 figures. The rule that allowed credits above 400% applied to tax years 2021 through 2025 only. The 2027 table runs to "not more than 400%," so a two-person household at exactly $86,560 stays inside the range. In our calculation, that household's contribution is 10.22% of income, or $737.20 a month, and an illustrative $1,000 benchmark with a $1,000 plan premium leaves a $262.80 monthly credit. Add $1 of income and the same household reaches 400.0046% of FPL, which removes the credit in the ordinary federal model. If your income sits near the line, run the calculator at both your low and high estimates before you count on the credit. The table shows an income window. It does not establish eligibility by itself. HealthCare.gov says income below 100% of FPL probably will not qualify for Marketplace savings but may qualify for Medicaid, and income below 138% may qualify for Medicaid in states that expanded it. The calculator covers households of 1 to 8 people in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia (DC). Poverty guidelines are higher in Alaska and Hawaii, and the 2026 table adds $5,680 for each person past eight. Households in either group should rely on the Marketplace application for their figure. The Benchmark and Your Chosen Plan The benchmark is the monthly premium for the second-lowest-cost Silver plan that applies to your coverage family, and it sets the size of the credit. Your chosen plan's premium, which the IRS calls the enrollment premium, acts only as a ceiling. The calculator asks for both numbers because they do different jobs in the formula. The IRS settles two edge cases for the benchmark. If only one Silver plan is available where you live, that plan counts as the second-lowest-cost Silver plan. If the two cheapest Silver plans cost the same, that shared premium is the benchmark. Tobacco use changes only one of the two inputs. The benchmark leaves out tobacco surcharges, so enter the non-tobacco price. The enrollment premium is the amount you are charged, so a tobacco user enters the higher plan price. The IRS gives an example of both rules. A $900 non-smoker benchmark is used even though smokers are quoted $1,200 for that plan. A tobacco user charged $650 for the chosen plan uses $650 as the enrollment premium, even though the non-tobacco price is $500. The ceiling comes into play when you pick a cheaper plan. If the benchmark minus your contribution is more than your plan's premium, the credit stops at that premium. The calculator has no ZIP code database and no built-in prices. Its $600 benchmark and $550 plan defaults are hypothetical numbers for the arithmetic. When you apply, the Marketplace estimates your credit from your family size, projected income, and other coverage, and the plan prices it shows are the figures to enter here. A Worked Federal Premium-Credit Calculation In our calculation, a two-person household with $50,000 of expected 2027 MAGI, a $600 benchmark, and a $550 chosen plan gets a $268.85 monthly federal credit and pays $281.15 a month. Both premiums are illustrative and come from no ZIP code quote. The arithmetic assumes every other eligibility condition is met. Step Figure 2026 FPL for 2 people $21,640 Income as % of FPL 231.05% Applicable percentage about 7.95% Yearly contribution $3,973.81 Monthly contribution $331.15 Benchmark minus contribution $600 minus $331.15 = $268.85 Cap check against the $550 plan $268.85 is under the cap Monthly credit $268.85 Net monthly premium $550 minus $268.85 = $281.15 A second case shows the premium cap. Use two people with $30,000 of MAGI, a $900 benchmark, and a $100 monthly plan premium. Assume every other eligibility condition is met, including that no one is eligible for Medicaid. Income is 138.63% of FPL, the applicable percentage is about 3.58%, and the monthly contribution is $89.61. The benchmark minus that contribution is far more than the $100 plan premium. The credit cannot exceed the $100 plan premium, so the credit is $100 and the net premium is $0. Read together, the two cases show how each input works. Income sets the contribution. When the ACA Subsidy Calculator Does Not Apply The calculator's figure does not apply to anyone eligible for government coverage that counts as qualifying health coverage, anyone with affordable employer coverage, or a household that fails the IRS filing rules. The calculator asks you to confirm these conditions before it shows a credit. Government coverage: a person eligible for Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) , Medicare, or another government program that counts as qualifying health coverage cannot get the credit for that person's Marketplace coverage. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count is an exception. Employer offers: an offer for 2027 plan years is generally affordable if the employee's self-only premium share is no more than 10.22% of household income. The test uses the lowest-cost plan that covers at least 60% of expected costs, and family members' offers apply the same percentage to the family premium. Employer enrollment: enrolling in an employer plan, including retiree coverage, blocks the credit even if that plan is unaffordable. Coverage from a former employer, including retiree coverage, can be declined, and the credit may still be available. Filing rules: married couples who file separately generally cannot claim the credit, with an exception for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. A person who can be claimed as a dependent by someone else cannot claim it. A new Medicaid rule starts January 1, 2027. HealthCare.gov says states that cover adults based on income alone may require a monthly work requirement for Medicaid. A person who lost or was denied Medicaid for not meeting that requirement may get Marketplace coverage but will not qualify for savings. Leave eligibility unconfirmed in the calculator to show an explanation instead of a credit. Limited Medicaid works differently. Some programs pay only for family planning, emergency treatment, or tuberculosis services. If your state's program does not count as qualifying health coverage , you may still get the premium tax credit when you meet the income and other rules. The calculator does not evaluate immigration status or state programs. Three facts can reverse an estimate: an affordable employer offer, eligibility for Medicaid or another government program that counts as qualifying coverage, and changes in law or plan prices. The official next step is a Marketplace application . HealthCare.gov says the application sends your information to your state if anyone in the household may qualify for Medicaid or CHIP. It also tells you whether you qualify for savings on a Marketplace plan. Updating Income Before Tax Reconciliation Advance payments of the premium tax credit are an estimate, and your final 2027 credit is figured on your tax return from actual household income and family size. If the advance payments were larger than the final credit, the IRS sets no repayment cap for tax years after 2025. The full difference reduces your refund or raises your balance due, and if the final credit is larger, the difference goes to you. Reporting changes to the Marketplace as soon as they happen lets it adjust your advance payments. The IRS lists these events among those that can change the credit: a lump-sum Social Security or Social Security Disability Insurance payment a taxable lump-sum distribution from an individual retirement account or other retirement arrangement capital gains from selling stocks, bonds, or cryptocurrency canceled debt, such as forgiven credit card debt marriage, divorce, a birth or adoption, or a move gaining or losing eligibility for employer or government coverage Filing a return is required. Anyone with advance payments must file a federal return with Form 8962 , and skipping that return ends advance payments in future years. Plan the premium around a range of incomes. Run the calculator at a low and a high 2027 income estimate, compare the two net premiums, and set aside the difference if your income can swing. Our guide on how to budget with irregular income covers health insurance costs without an employer plan, and you can put the premium in a household budget . The estimate requires a correct benchmark premium and annual MAGI. Take-home pay alone cannot establish annual MAGI. An affordable employer offer, qualifying government coverage, or changed law or plan prices can reverse it. Compare income scenarios in the ACA subsidy calculator, then update your Marketplace application whenever your income changes. Frequently Asked Questions What is ACA subsidy based on? The ACA premium tax credit is based on expected household modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) compared with the federal poverty level for your household size, plus the benchmark Silver premium for your coverage family. The income sets your contribution, the benchmark minus that contribution sets the credit, and the premium of the plan you enroll in caps it. How to qualify for ACA subsidy? You must meet every IRS eligibility condition. Income alone cannot establish eligibility. Household income must fall in the allowed range. Married filing separately generally prevents the credit, with a limited abuse or abandonment exception. No one else can claim you as a dependent. The covered person must enroll in a non-catastrophic Marketplace plan and lack affordable employer coverage. Eligibility for qualifying government coverage, such as most Medicaid or Medicare, prevents the credit. Limited-benefit Medicaid that does not count as qualifying coverage is an exception. The covered person must pay the share of premiums the credit does not cover. What is the maximum ACA subsidy? The ACA subsidy can be as large as the full premium of the plan you enroll in, because the IRS caps the credit at enrollment premiums. Below that cap, the size depends on how far the benchmark premium exceeds your income-based contribution. In our lower-income example, two people with $30,000 of MAGI, a $900 benchmark, and a $100 plan get a $100 credit and pay $0, assuming every other eligibility condition is met. What are the ACA subsidy income limits? For 2027 coverage, the ordinary range is 100% to 400% of the 2026 federal poverty level in the 48 contiguous states and DC. That is $15,960 to $63,840 for one person, $21,640 to $86,560 for two, and $33,000 to $132,000 for four. Alaska and Hawaii use higher poverty guidelines, and income inside the range does not establish eligibility on its own. Is ACA subsidy based on adjusted gross income? The ACA subsidy is based on modified adjusted gross income, which starts with adjusted gross income from line 11 of Form 1040. You add untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits, and tax-exempt interest, and you leave out Supplemental Security Income. For many people the two figures are the same or very close. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. You can estimate SNAP food benefits separately from cash income because SNAP can pay only for eligible food. Add up all reliable take-home income — both partners' paychecks plus any steady side income — then list shared and personal expenses across needs, wants, and savings. The calculator applies the 50/30/20 rule to your combined income: 50% for needs like housing, utilities, groceries, transportation, insurance, and minimum debt payments; 30% for wants; and 20% for savings and debt payoff. For families, the savings bucket often carries extra weight — an emergency fund sized to household expenses, retirement for two, and goals like a 529 college account. Because households have more moving parts, the most useful habit is a monthly review where both partners see the same numbers, comparing each bucket's actual spending against its target the same way our budget variance guide explains for a business budget. Once you know your savings target, plan the bigger picture: check your net worth and stay on track for retirement . A worked example Consider a two-income household bringing home $7,500 a month. The 50/30/20 rule sets targets of $3,750 for needs, $2,250 for wants, and $1,500 for savings. This family's actual needs — mortgage, utilities, groceries, two commutes, insurance, and minimum debts — come to $4,350, about $600 over the needs target and 58% of income. Their wants run light at $1,300, and they put $1,800 toward savings, a 24% savings rate. Because the wants bucket has room, the household still saves above 20% and ends the month with $50 left to assign — a healthy plan even though needs run high, which is typical for families in higher-cost areas. Common mistakes to avoid Counting income you don't reliably receive. Budget steady take-home pay; treat bonuses and variable side income as extra. Tracking only one partner's spending. A household budget needs every account and card in the picture. Underbudgeting kid-related costs — childcare, activities, and growing grocery bills add up fast. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) bases the 30% share on the expectation that SNAP households spend about 30% of their own resources on food. For FY2027 in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia, the maximum allotment runs from $306 for one person to $1,841 for eight. The calculator above works through six steps in this order: Add earned income and unearned income, such as Social Security, to get gross monthly income. Subtract 20% of earned income. Subtract the standard deduction for your household size. Subtract dependent care, child support where your state allows it, and medical costs over $35 for an elderly or disabled member. Subtract the part of shelter costs above half of that adjusted income, up to $769 unless a member is elderly or disabled. Multiply net income by 0.3, round up, and subtract the result from the maximum allotment. The calculator labels its result as conditional because the formula only pays out once a state agency finds the household eligible. When net income lands above the federal net income limit for your household size, the calculator holds back a benefit amount unless you confirm that a state agency has already found the household eligible. FY2027 sets a $25 minimum for eligible one- or two-person households. The calculator shows that $25 floor on its own line, and it never turns a failed income screen into an award. The calculator covers households of 1 to 8 people in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia. Households in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, or the U.S. Virgin Islands, and households of nine or more, get no estimate here and should use the FY2027 allotment and deduction tables instead. You can copy or download the result with your inputs, and nothing you type is sent to a server. Income and Deductions for the SNAP Benefits Calculator Enter your household's monthly gross income in two parts, earned and unearned, because the 20% deduction applies to earned income. Wages go in the earned field. Social Security goes in the unearned field. Then enter the deductions SNAP allows. FNA lists these for FY2027: A standard deduction of $217 for 1 to 3 people, $229 for 4, $268 for 5, and $308 for 6 or more, which the calculator applies from your household size. Dependent care costs when the care is needed for work, training, or education. Legally owed child support payments, in states that allow this deduction. Medical costs for an elderly or disabled member above $35 a month, when insurance or someone else does not pay them. Excess shelter costs, explained below. Shelter costs include rent or mortgage payments, mortgage interest, and taxes on the home, so put property taxes in the housing field if you pay them. Allowable utility costs are heating and cooking fuel, electricity, water, and the basic fee for one telephone. Some states allow a set amount for utilities in place of actual bills. FNA does not publish one national figure for that set amount, so the utility field starts at $0. Enter only the utility amount your state SNAP agency approves, and do not add actual bills on top of it. Households experiencing homelessness can get a standard $205.66 homeless shelter deduction. The calculator has no field for it, so ask your agency through the SNAP state directory how it applies to your case. A household where every member receives Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), Supplemental Security Income (SSI), or in some places general assistance may be categorically eligible. Most states also use broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), which lets a state align SNAP income and resource limits with its TANF-funded programs. SNAP Benefits for Older or Disabled Members SNAP changes the benefit math in three ways when a household includes a member who is elderly or disabled: The gross income test does not apply. The net income limit still applies. Medical costs above $35 a month that insurance or someone else does not pay count as a deduction. The excess shelter deduction has no $769 cap, so all shelter costs above half of adjusted income come off. Turn on the elderly or disabled setting in the calculator to apply the medical deduction and the uncapped shelter deduction. Your state SNAP agency subtracts allowed deductions from your gross income to get net income, multiplies net income by 0.3, rounds up, and subtracts that amount from the maximum allotment for your household size. For a four-person household with $856.50 in net income, that is $1,023 minus $257, or $766 for a full month. What is the minimum SNAP benefit? Other areas use the amounts in the FY2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) tables . The minimum applies only after a household is found eligible. How much can you get in SNAP benefits? Households of nine or more can check the FY2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) tables . Subtract 30% of net income, rounded up to the next whole dollar, from the maximum allotment. An otherwise eligible household with $0 net income receives the full maximum. What are SNAP benefits income limits? For FY2027, most households in the 48 contiguous states and the District of Columbia need to meet both the gross limit of 130% of the poverty level and the net limit of 100%. For four people, that is $3,575 gross and $2,750 net. Households with an elderly or disabled member only need to meet the net limit, and states using broad-based categorical eligibility can align limits with their TANF-funded programs. Can seniors get food stamps? Yes, people age 60 or older can get SNAP when their household meets the program rules, and special rules apply to them. A household with a member who is 60 or older or disabled only has to meet the net income limit, can deduct medical costs over $35 a month, and has no cap on the excess shelter deduction. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) describes the Marketplace as the place to find private health insurance options, buy a plan, and get help with premiums and out-of-pocket costs for those who are eligible. Monthly premiums for a Marketplace plan go directly to the insurance company. Medicaid and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) provide free or low-cost coverage to eligible low-income adults, families and children, pregnant women, the elderly, and people with disabilities, according to HealthCare.gov. Medicaid programs must follow federal guidelines, but eligible income levels, coverage and costs differ from state to state. Some Medicaid programs pay for care directly, and others use private insurance companies to provide Medicaid coverage. Benefits also follow different rules. Full-benefit Medicaid benefits differ by state, though HealthCare.gov says all states provide comprehensive coverage. Every Marketplace plan covers 10 benefit categories, including prescription drugs, emergency services, hospitalization, laboratory services, and mental health and substance use disorder services, along with pre-existing conditions and free preventive services from in-network providers. Marketplace plans and full-benefit Medicaid count as qualifying health coverage. HealthCare.gov lists Marketplace plans, Medicaid and CHIP among the coverage types that meet the law's minimum requirements for comprehensive health coverage. Advertise With Us → ACA vs Medicaid Eligibility and Savings Eligibility for full-benefit Medicaid generally prevents a person from receiving federal premium savings on a Marketplace plan. The IRS lists this as a premium tax credit condition: the person enrolled in Marketplace coverage must not be eligible for coverage through a government program such as Medicaid or CHIP. HealthCare.gov puts it plainly: "If you qualify for Medicaid, you aren't eligible for savings on a Marketplace plan." Declining Medicaid does not restore the savings. A person eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP who keeps a Marketplace plan generally pays full price for the premium and for covered services. A child may also lose CHIP eligibility if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is one exception. Some limited types of Medicaid pay only for family planning, treatment of an emergency medical condition, or tuberculosis services. When a Medicaid program does not count as minimum essential coverage, the person may be eligible for premium tax credits and other Marketplace savings if they qualify based on income and other criteria. HealthCare.gov's Medicaid minimum essential coverage lookup shows, by state, whether a given Medicaid program counts and what action to take. People with limited Medicaid can also fill out a Marketplace application to find out whether they qualify for full-benefit Medicaid or a Marketplace plan with savings. Medicaid status is one of several federal tests. The IRS lists these premium tax credit requirements: Household income generally from 100 percent to 400 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL) for the family size. A filing status other than married filing separately, apart from a special rule for certain victims of domestic abuse or spousal abandonment. Not being claimable as a dependent by another person. No access to affordable employer coverage that provides minimum value for the person enrolled. Payment of the share of premiums not covered by advance credit payments. A timing rule applies when status changes mid-year. The Marketplace may find someone ineligible for Medicaid at enrollment and approve advance credit payments. In that case, the IRS generally treats the person as ineligible for Medicaid for the rest of the plan year, even if Medicaid later approves coverage. The IRS still tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately. ACA vs Medicaid Income Rules Household income alone does not decide whether a person gets Medicaid or Marketplace savings, because state rules and personal categories change the result. HealthCare.gov says each state's coverage options consider income, household size, family status such as pregnancy or caring for young children, disability, age and other factors. Some states expanded Medicaid to cover adults below a certain income level, and others did not. HealthCare.gov advises applying for Medicaid even when income looks too high. That advice applies especially to people who have children, are pregnant or have a disability. The federal poverty level is a yearly income measure used for both programs. HealthCare.gov's federal poverty level table lists 2026 amounts of $15,960 for one person and $33,000 for a family of four, with higher amounts in Alaska and Hawaii. Under HealthCare.gov's general bands, income below 138 percent of FPL may qualify for Medicaid in an expansion state. Income below 100 percent probably will not qualify for Marketplace savings but may qualify for Medicaid. Marketplace savings use expected household modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). Medicaid income rules vary by state and eligibility category. HealthCare.gov's income guide defines MAGI as adjusted gross income plus untaxed foreign income, non-taxable Social Security benefits and tax-exempt interest, without Supplemental Security Income. Marketplace savings are based on expected household income for the coverage year rather than last year's income. Self-employed applicants count the income they expect to make from the business after expenses. For income that is hard to predict, HealthCare.gov says to report current income, review the yearly estimate it shows, and update the application as changes happen. For tax years after 2025, the IRS applies no repayment cap. The full amount of advance credit payments above the allowed credit is added to the tax bill. Members of one household can end up in different programs. HealthCare.gov notes that children may qualify for CHIP even when a parent does not qualify for Medicaid. In many cases, a parent who qualifies for Marketplace savings will have children who qualify for Medicaid or CHIP. Applying Through the Marketplace or Your State A household can apply for Medicaid through a Marketplace application or directly through its state Medicaid agency, and either route can lead to the other program. On a Marketplace application, if anyone in the household looks eligible for Medicaid or CHIP, the Marketplace securely sends that information to the state agency, which then contacts the household about enrollment. The same Marketplace application shows whether anyone qualifies for cost savings on a Marketplace plan. The direct route starts with the state. HealthCare.gov's Medicaid and CHIP coverage page lists contact information for each state's Medicaid agency. A state denial feeds back into the Marketplace. In most cases, the state securely sends the person's contact information to the Marketplace, which mails a letter about Marketplace coverage. A denied applicant can apply and enroll in Marketplace coverage without waiting for that letter. Enrollment timing differs between the two: Medicaid and CHIP: apply any time of year, and coverage can start immediately. Marketplace Open Enrollment: November 1 to January 15. Enroll by December 15 for coverage that starts January 1, or by January 15 for coverage that starts February 1. Marketplace outside Open Enrollment: a qualifying life change opens a Special Enrollment Period. Medicaid may also help pay for medical care from the last 3 months, even before enrollment. Payment depends on the family's income and medical expenses at the time care was received. Marketplace applications can be filed online, by phone, with help from someone in the community, through an agent or broker, through certified enrollment partner websites, or on paper. HealthCare.gov offers a checklist of what to gather before applying on its Marketplace quick guide . Rules to Check for 2027 Coverage Two rule changes shape 2027 coverage decisions: a Medicaid work requirement in some states and immigration-status rules for full Medicaid and Marketplace savings. Both notices appear on HealthCare.gov's Medicaid and CHIP coverage page and its Marketplace quick guide . Starting January 1, 2027, adults in states that provide Medicaid based on income alone may need to meet a new monthly work requirement to qualify for Medicaid or keep it. HealthCare.gov says a person who lost or was denied Medicaid for not meeting the state's work requirement may get Marketplace coverage. That person will not qualify for savings to lower Marketplace plan costs. After an ordinary Medicaid denial, by contrast, HealthCare.gov says a person may qualify for the premium tax credit or other cost savings. The reason for a Medicaid denial therefore matters for the Marketplace budget. A household comparing plans after a work-requirement denial should expect full-price premiums when estimating monthly costs. For noncitizen applicants, HealthCare.gov lists these immigration statuses for full Medicaid or CHIP coverage following a law change: Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR, Green Card holder) Cuban or Haitian entrant Compact of Free Association (COFA) migrant Depending on the state, lawfully residing pregnant women and children may also be eligible for full Medicaid or CHIP. For noncitizens applying for Marketplace plans, only certain immigration statuses qualify for savings starting January 1, 2027. People with other statuses may still be eligible for Marketplace coverage without savings. For 2027 Marketplace coverage starting January 1, the enrollment deadline is December 15. Medicaid applications remain open year-round. The Next Step Before Choosing a Plan The next step is an official eligibility result for each person in the household, from a Marketplace application on HealthCare.gov or from the state Medicaid agency. That result answers the ACA vs Medicaid question person by person. Full-benefit Medicaid eligibility generally removes Marketplace savings. Limited-benefit Medicaid, an ordinary Medicaid denial and a work-requirement denial can lead to different savings outcomes. Neither option is the better choice for every household, because eligibility rules decide which coverage comes with financial help. If the result points to a Marketplace plan, compare each plan's monthly premium and provider network in the Marketplace before enrolling. A Marketplace plan starts only after the first premium is paid, if there is one. If you already have coverage, confirm replacement coverage before ending the existing plan. If Medicaid is approved while a Marketplace plan is active, HealthCare.gov says to end the Marketplace plan when Medicaid starts, unless you tell the state agency you want to keep both. Once the premium is known, plan the monthly premium alongside other bills. If income changes month to month, budget insurance with irregular income . Update your Marketplace income estimate whenever expected income changes, then check how that affects your ACA vs Medicaid coverage. Frequently Asked Questions What is Obamacare insurance? Obamacare is another name for the Affordable Care Act (ACA), a law. Marketplace plans are private health insurance bought through the Health Insurance Marketplace. Every Marketplace plan covers 10 benefit categories, including prescription drugs, emergency services and hospitalization, and covers pre-existing conditions. Depending on expected household income, a buyer may qualify for a premium tax credit that lowers the monthly premium, plus extra savings on deductibles, copayments and coinsurance. Medicaid is a separate public program run jointly by the federal government and the states. What is a coverage gap in health insurance? In a state that has not expanded Medicaid, a coverage gap means some adults cannot get Medicaid or ordinary Marketplace savings. HealthCare.gov describes adults below 100% of the federal poverty level who do not qualify under their state's Medicaid rules. Their incomes are too high for Medicaid in their state and too low for ordinary Marketplace savings. A 2027 Medicaid work-requirement denial can also prevent Marketplace savings, but it follows a separate rule. Still apply, because state categories and other factors can change the outcome. What disqualifies you for Medicaid? No single factor disqualifies everyone, because each state sets its own Medicaid income levels and categories within federal guidelines. Income above a category's limit can prevent Medicaid eligibility. For noncitizen applicants, immigration status also affects full-coverage eligibility. A state that has not expanded Medicaid may offer fewer coverage options. Starting January 1, 2027, adults in states that cover people based on income alone may lose or be denied Medicaid for not meeting a monthly work requirement. HealthCare.gov still recommends applying when income looks too high, especially for people with children, a pregnancy or a disability. Is ACA or Medicaid better? Neither is better for every household, because eligibility rules decide which option comes with financial help. A person eligible for full-benefit Medicaid gets free or low-cost coverage there, and would generally pay full price for a Marketplace plan. A person denied Medicaid for ordinary reasons may qualify for a premium tax credit on a Marketplace plan, while a 2027 work-requirement denial allows Marketplace coverage without savings. Full-benefit Medicaid coverage differs by state. Every state provides comprehensive full-benefit coverage, and every Marketplace plan covers the same 10 benefit categories. Compare actual premiums and provider networks after the eligibility result arrives. Can you have Medicaid and Marketplace insurance at the same time? Yes, a person can keep both, but full-benefit Medicaid generally means paying full price for the Marketplace plan premium and covered services. HealthCare.gov says to tell the state agency if you want to keep both, and notes that a child may no longer qualify for CHIP if the family keeps the Marketplace plan. Limited-benefit Medicaid is different: a person may still qualify for Marketplace savings based on income and other factors. The IRS tells anyone who may be enrolled in both Medicaid and a Marketplace plan with advance credit payments to contact the Marketplace immediately. A family that qualifies for both programs can receive both at the same time. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) loads monthly grocery benefits for a whole household onto an Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) card. The Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) serves pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding participants, infants, and children under 5. It provides specific healthy foods, nutrition education, breastfeeding support and referrals. For a household that fits both programs, the practical answer is to file two separate applications. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) publishes the federal rules for both programs. Applications go to different offices: a state SNAP agency for SNAP and a local WIC agency for WIC. The table below draws on four USDA pages: SNAP eligibility , what SNAP can buy , WIC eligibility and WIC benefits . Three differences in the table decide which application a family needs: Who qualifies. SNAP looks at the household, which applies in its own state and must meet income limits, resource limits and other program rules. WIC first asks whether someone is pregnant, up to 6 months postpartum, breastfeeding up to the infant's first birthday, an infant, or a child up to the fifth birthday. What the card buys. A SNAP EBT card buys any food for the household at authorized stores, with listed exclusions. The WIC benefit card buys foods on the WIC list at WIC-approved retailers. What comes with the food. SNAP provides a monthly grocery allotment. WIC adds one-on-one nutrition counseling, breastfeeding support and referrals to health and community services, all at no cost to the family. A household with no pregnant, postpartum or breastfeeding member, no infant and no child under 5 has no one WIC can enroll. For that household, SNAP is the program to check. A household with at least one of those members can check both. Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Who it serves Households that meet their state's SNAP income limits, resource limits and other program rules People who are pregnant, postpartum (up to 6 months after a pregnancy ends) or breastfeeding (up to the infant's first birthday), plus infants and children up to their fifth birthday Household definition Everyone who lives together and buys and prepares meals together; spouses and most children under 22 count even if they eat separately Everyone you live with and share income and expenses with; a pregnant member adds one to household size for each expected birth Benefit form Monthly allotment on an EBT card that works like a debit card at authorized food stores Benefits for WIC-listed foods on a WIC benefit card used at WIC-approved retailers Foods and services Any food for the household, excluding alcohol, tobacco, hot foods, vitamins, supplements and nonfood items Specified healthy foods plus personalized nutrition education, breastfeeding support and referrals to health and community services Application route State SNAP agency where you live; interview and proof of information, with a decision notice in most cases within 30 days Local WIC agency in your area; WIC staff complete a free nutrition assessment before enrollment 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Eligible Families Can Receive Both A family enrolled in SNAP can also enroll in WIC, and SNAP receipt may already satisfy the WIC income requirement. If you or children in your care receive Medicaid, SNAP or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), you may already be income eligible for WIC. The USDA WIC eligibility page says those applicants can skip the WIC income chart. Income is only one of the WIC requirements USDA lists. SNAP receipt does not settle the other three: Participant category. The person enrolling must be pregnant, postpartum, breastfeeding, an infant or a child under 5. Location. You apply through a WIC agency in your area, and some areas offer more than one way to apply, including online. Nutrition assessment. Every applicant receives a free, simple health check from WIC staff before enrollment, and WIC uses that information to personalize benefits and services. The California WIC Program states that only staff at a local WIC office can officially confirm that a family qualifies. A current SNAP case can cover the income step of WIC screening, and local WIC staff decide the rest at the appointment. The reverse path works differently. A WIC family that wants SNAP applies with its state SNAP agency. SNAP vs WIC Household Rules SNAP and WIC define a household differently, so the same family can report a different household size to each program. For SNAP, USDA groups everyone who lives together and buys and prepares meals together as one household. Spouses and most children under age 22 who live together count as one SNAP household even if they buy and prepare meals separately. Other SNAP rules affect separate-household status and eligibility for people receiving institutional meals. A person 60 or older who cannot buy and prepare meals separately because of a permanent disability may form a separate SNAP household with a spouse. The separate-household exception requires the other people in the home to have income no higher than 165% of the poverty level. A person who gets most meals from an institution is normally not eligible, with exceptions for elderly and disabled people. For WIC, the household is everyone you live with and share income and expenses with. USDA's WIC page says this includes children, people you are not related to, students away at college, and military service members away on active duty. If someone in the household is pregnant, household size goes up by one for each expected birth. Counting a person in the WIC household size does not make that person a WIC participant. In California, WIC completes a nutrition assessment for each qualifying family member and loads food benefits for those qualifying members onto the California WIC Card. Household size sets the income limit in both programs. USDA sets the SNAP gross monthly income limit at 130% of poverty for applications from Oct. 1, 2026, through Sept. 30, 2027. In the 48 contiguous states, the District of Columbia, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands, that limit is $2,345 for two people, $2,960 for three and $3,575 for four, with higher limits in Alaska and Hawaii. Most SNAP households must also pass a net income test after deductions such as 20% of earned income, a standard deduction and dependent care costs needed for work, training or education. WIC counts household income before deductions or taxes, including wages and tips, Social Security, child support, unemployment benefits and retirement payments. WIC leaves out loans, AmeriCorps income and certain military pay such as Basic Allowance for Housing and combat pay. The USDA WIC page shows income limits after you select a household size and state. SNAP vs WIC Food Benefits SNAP pays for food for the whole household, while WIC pays for a set list of healthy foods for each participant along with nutrition services. Both benefits arrive on cards that work like debit cards at approved stores: an EBT card for SNAP and a WIC benefit card for WIC. The state agency then holds an eligibility interview, asks for proof of what you reported, and in most cases sends you a notice with its decision within 30 days. USAGov describes SNAP as the program known previously as "food stamps," which can help you pay for food if you have a low income. If your household needs food right away, ask the state agency about expedited service, which can deliver benefits within 7 days to households that meet extra requirements. Tools for this journey Household Budget Calculator → On This Page Apply for Food Stamps in These Steps What to Have Ready for the SNAP Application Apply for Food Stamps Online or With Help What Happens After You Apply When to Ask About Expedited SNAP Service If Your Notice or Application Needs Follow-Up The Next Step for Your Food Budget Apply for Food Stamps in These Steps You apply for food stamps through the SNAP agency in the state where you currently live, and the process runs in six steps: Find your state agency. Open the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) state directory and click your state, or New York City, for contact and application information. Get your state's application. Each state has its own form. If your state's form is not on the web, contact your local SNAP office and ask for one. Submit it through a method your state accepts. Depending on the state, USAGov lists online, in person, by mail and by fax as ways you may be able to submit. Keep a dated confirmation. If you are found eligible, benefits count back to the date you submitted your application. Complete the eligibility interview. The interview is typically done over the telephone or in person. Send the proof the state agency requests, then read its notice. In most cases the notice saying whether you are eligible arrives within 30 days of your application. A SNAP calculator or screener result does not file an application. Submit your state's application through one of the agency's accepted methods. FNA's eligibility page says a member of your household must contact the state agency directly to apply, because each state has a different form and process. FNA itself does not process applications. What to Have Ready for the SNAP Application Have records ready for the facts SNAP uses to decide eligibility: who lives in your household, your income, your resources and certain expenses. Your state agency asks for the proof it needs during the verification step. Treat the table as a preparation checklist. Your state's verification request is the official list. What to gather Which SNAP rule it relates to Names of everyone who lives with you and buys and prepares meals with you People who live together and purchase and prepare meals together form one SNAP household. Spouses and most children under 22 are included even if they shop and cook separately. Recent pay records for each working member Gross monthly income is compared with the limit for your household size, and earned income gets a 20% deduction. Records of other income, such as Social Security Gross income is total non-excluded income before deductions. FNA's own worked example adds Social Security to earned income. Bank statements and a count of cash on hand Countable resources such as cash or money in a bank account are limited to $3,000, or $4,750 if a member is 60 or older or disabled. Vehicle details, including any amount owed Vehicles count as resources, and each state determines how they count. Rent or mortgage, property tax, utility and phone bills These feed the excess shelter deduction for shelter costs above half of income after other deductions. Child or dependent care costs A dependent care deduction applies when care is needed for work, training or education. Medical bills for members 60 or older or disabled Costs above $35 a month that insurance or someone else does not pay can be deducted. Records of legally owed child support you pay This is a deduction in some states. The expense records matter because deductions lower your net income. In most cases a household must meet both a gross and a net income limit, while a household with an elderly or disabled member only has to meet the net limit. For applications from Oct. 1, 2026, through Sept. 30, 2027, the gross monthly income limit in the 48 contiguous states, the District of Columbia, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands is $1,729 for one person, $2,345 for two, $2,960 for three and $3,575 for four. Those figures come from FNA's cost-of-living page , and the limits are higher in Alaska and Hawaii. Depending on your state, you may be able to have more resources than the federal limits and still be eligible. Apply for Food Stamps Online or With Help You can apply online when your state agency offers an online application, which FNA says some states do on the agency website. FNA lists three ways to reach your state agency: Visit your local SNAP office. Go to your state agency's website, where some states offer the online application. Call your state's toll-free SNAP Information hotline. Start from the FNA state directory so the website, phone number and form you use belong to your state agency. ModernWallet cannot file an application, check a case or collect application details for you. If you cannot go to or call your local SNAP office, or you have no internet access, another person can act as your authorized representative. That person can apply and be interviewed on your behalf. You must name the authorized representative in writing. For a general government question, USAGov offers free help from a real person at 1-844-USAGOV1 (1-844-872-4681). USAGov answers the question or tells you where to find the answer. Your state agency still handles the SNAP application itself. What Happens After You Apply After you apply, your state agency or local SNAP office processes the application and, in most cases, sends you a notice within 30 days saying whether you are eligible. During those 30 days you complete an eligibility interview and give proof of the information you reported. If you are found eligible, you receive benefits based on the date you submitted your application. That rule is the reason to keep a dated confirmation from the day you file. The benefit amount comes from the state's decision, so treat any calculator figure as an estimate until the notice arrives. Approved benefits arrive on an Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) card, which works like a debit card. Benefits load into the account each month, and you use the card to buy groceries at authorized food stores and retailers. Each state has a benefit issuance schedule showing when benefits become available. Your approval notice also states your certification period, which is how long you will receive SNAP. Before that period ends, you get another notice saying you must recertify to keep receiving benefits. When to Ask About Expedited SNAP Service Ask about expedited service if your household has very little income and cash, because qualifying households may receive SNAP benefits within 7 days of the application date. FNA gives two examples of households that may meet the additional requirements: Less than $100 in liquid resources and $150 in monthly gross income. Combined monthly gross income and liquid resources that are less than what the household pays each month for rent or mortgage and utilities. To see whether the second example might describe you, add your household's monthly gross income to its liquid resources. Then compare that total with your monthly rent or mortgage plus utilities. If the total is lower, ask the state agency about expedited service. These are FNA's examples, and your state agency decides whether your household meets the requirements. FNA tells applicants to contact the state agency for additional details. Answer any interview or proof request the state agency sends while it reviews you. If Your Notice or Application Needs Follow-Up Every follow-up on a SNAP application goes through your state agency, because FNA does not process applications or have access to case information. Match what you receive to the action in this table: What you see What to do Application submitted, no word yet Keep your dated confirmation and contact your state agency for the status of your application. Interview scheduled Complete the interview by phone or in person, as the state agency arranges. Request for proof Send the requested proof to the state agency. Food needed right away Ask the state agency about expedited service. Approval notice Note your certification period and watch for your EBT card. Denial or a decision you disagree with Request a fair hearing within 90 days of the decision. Recertification notice Follow your local SNAP office's instructions to recertify before the certification period ends. A fair hearing puts your case in front of an official who is required by law to review the facts fairly and objectively. Request a fair hearing by phone, in writing or at your SNAP office. A fair hearing cannot change SNAP laws or regulations, but it can make sure the decision on your case was made correctly. Once benefits start, you can see your EBT balance on many store receipts, in a state mobile app if your state offers one, or by contacting your SNAP office. The Next Step for Your Food Budget Once the notice arrives, record the actual SNAP award as its own line in your budget, apart from your cash income. The benefit sits on an EBT card used for groceries at authorized stores, so it belongs against your grocery spending. To build that plan, make a budget from actual statements and use the Household Budget Calculator to plan household spending separately from food benefits . Keep copies of the pay, bank and bill records you gathered, so you have them ready when the state asks for updated information or sends a recertification notice. Your state agency decides eligibility and the award amount, and FNA adjusts income limits and maximum allotments at the start of each federal fiscal year on Oct. 1. Open the FNA state directory now, choose your state and apply for food stamps on that agency's own application. Frequently Asked Questions What documents are needed to apply for food stamps? Your state agency decides which documents it needs and asks for them during verification. Gather records for household members, income, bank balances, vehicles, housing and utility costs, dependent care, child support you pay and medical costs for members 60 or older or disabled. Can you apply for food stamps online? Yes, if your state offers an online application. FNA says some states have online applications on the state agency website, and USAGov lists online, in person, mail and fax as possible methods depending on the state. Find your state's own site through the FNA state directory . Can I apply for food stamps over the phone? Your state agency decides which submission methods it accepts, and the eligibility interview is typically completed by telephone or in person. Ask your state SNAP agency whether you can file by telephone, and keep the filing confirmation. Who can apply for food stamps? A member of the household applies in the state where the household currently lives. To receive benefits, the household must meet requirements that include income and resource limits, which update each year. SNAP work requirements and non-citizen eligibility rules have changed. The official eligibility page is being updated with those changes. Where can I apply for food stamps in person? Apply in person at your local SNAP office. The FNA state directory gives contact and application information for each state and New York City. If you cannot get to the office, a person you name in writing can apply and be interviewed for you as your authorized representative. mainEntity.name: What documents are needed to apply for food stamps?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your state agency decides which documents it needs and asks for them during verification. Gather records for household members, income, bank balances, vehicles, housing and utility costs, dependent care, child support you pay and medical costs for members 60 or older or disabled.

mainEntity.name: Can you apply for food stamps online?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if your state offers an online application. FNA says some states have online applications on the state agency website, and USAGov lists online, in person, mail and fax as possible methods depending on the state. Find your state's own site through the FNA state directory.

mainEntity.name: Can I apply for food stamps over the phone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your state agency decides which submission methods it accepts, and the eligibility interview is typically completed by telephone or in person. Ask your state SNAP agency whether you can file by telephone, and keep the filing confirmation.

mainEntity.name: Who can apply for food stamps?

acceptedAnswer.text: A member of the household applies in the state where the household currently lives. To receive benefits, the household must meet requirements that include income and resource limits, which update each year. SNAP work requirements and non-citizen eligibility rules have changed. The official eligibility page is being updated with those changes.

mainEntity.name: Where can I apply for food stamps in person?

acceptedAnswer.text: Apply in person at your local SNAP office. The FNA state directory gives contact and application information for each state and New York City. If you cannot get to the office, a person you name in writing can apply and be interviewed for you as your authorized representative.

If you're a freelancer earning between $2,800 and $6,200 a month, base your core spending on $2,800. Then use anything above that for taxes, a buffer fund, and retirement savings. This guide explains how to choose a realistic baseline, calculate the size of your buffer fund, pay quarterly estimated taxes, and cover health care and retirement without an employer plan. Tools for this journey Zero-Based Budget Calculator → Monthly Budget Calculator → Household Budget Calculator → How to Calculate Net Worth → How Do You Find a Realistic Baseline Income When Pay Changes Every Month? Your baseline income is the lowest month you can realistically expect, not the average of all your months. Pull your last 12 months of take-home pay and sort them from low to high. Use the lowest month, or the average of your three lowest months, as the number your fixed budget is built on. Suppose a freelance designer earns between $2,800 and $6,200 a month. Over 12 months, her income adds up to $52,000, which averages to $4,333 a month. But four of those months come in under $4,000, and her single lowest month is $2,800. If she builds her budget around the $4,333 average, she falls short four months out of the year. Building around $2,800 — the amount she can always count on — means rent and bills get paid even in a slow month. Extra income above that baseline becomes bonus money, not a hole to fill. How Do You Build a Zero-Based Budget Around a Baseline Number? A zero-based budget assigns every dollar of your baseline income a job before the month starts. List fixed costs first — rent, insurance, minimum debt payments — then variable essentials like groceries and gas. Every dollar of the baseline gets assigned somewhere, so nothing is left unaccounted for. ModernWallet's zero-based budget calculator is built for exactly this situation, since it forces income minus expenses to equal zero. Run it using your baseline number, not last month's actual income. That way the plan holds up even in your worst month, not just your best one. If income swings by category — more client work some months, more retail hours in others — track categories separately. The monthly budget calculator and household budget calculator both handle this well. Rebuild the plan whenever your baseline shifts, such as after adding a new recurring client. A baseline budget is a living document, not a one-time worksheet. How Should a Buffer Fund Be Sized for Income That Goes Up and Down? A buffer fund for irregular income needs two separate numbers, not one flat multiple of expenses. The first is a smoothing buffer, sized to the income gap you expect several times a year. The second is a true emergency reserve: three to six months of your baseline expenses, for total loss of income. Going back to the designer earning $2,800 to $6,200, her average month is $4,333 and her baseline is $2,800. That's a gap of about $1,533 a month. If she typically has four low months a year, her smoothing buffer needs roughly $6,133 to cover that gap. On top of the smoothing buffer, she also needs a true emergency reserve for total income loss. That reserve should hold three to six months of her $2,800 baseline, or $8,400 to $16,800. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes the right fund size depends on your own spending patterns and income stability. Someone with steadier, higher-floor income needs a smaller reserve than someone whose income swings hard every month. How Do Quarterly Estimated Taxes Work for Self-Employed Income? Self-employed workers must pay estimated tax if they expect to owe $1,000 or more for the year. The IRS requires these payments in four installments, because no employer withholds tax from freelance or gig income. Payments are due in April, June, September, and the following January. To avoid a penalty, pay at least 90% of this year's tax, or 100% of last year's tax. High earners — those with prior-year adjusted gross income over $150,000 — must pay 110% instead of 100%. Most freelancers find the prior-year rule easier, since it skips guessing this year's income. A simple habit: set aside a fixed share of every payment you receive in a separate tax account, and move it out of checking the same day a client pays you, before it feels like spending money. The right share is narrower than the 25% to 30% rule of thumb suggests — it depends on your profit and on whether you also have a job, since freelance income stacks on top of a salary at your top marginal rate. Our guide to how much to set aside for taxes works out the figure for your own situation. It covers both income tax and self-employment tax, which funds Social Security and Medicare. How Do Freelancers Budget for Health Insurance Without an Employer Plan? Freelancers without an employer plan can buy coverage through the ACA Health Insurance Marketplace at HealthCare.gov . Premiums depend on your income, age, and state, and many self-employed workers qualify for subsidies that lower the monthly cost. Because your income changes, you report your estimated net self-employment income for the year, not last year's number. Build the premium into your baseline budget as a fixed cost, the same as rent. If your income rises well above your estimate, update your Marketplace application, since a higher income can change your subsidy. Waiting until tax time to reconcile a big gap can mean owing money back. Some freelancers also budget a separate line for deductibles and copays, especially with a high-deductible plan. Treat this like the buffer fund: a specific amount, kept separate from daily spending money. Use the calculator to estimate a federal premium credit and compare Marketplace coverage with Medicaid before planning your coverage costs. How Can Self-Employed Workers Save for Retirement Without a 401(k) Match? Self-employed workers can save for retirement using a SEP-IRA or a solo 401(k) instead of an employer plan. A SEP-IRA lets you contribute up to 25% of net self-employment earnings, capped by the IRS each year. A solo 401(k) allows similar limits and can also accept smaller Roth contributions, depending on the provider. Without an employer match, the incentive to save has to come from your own budget. A workable rule: contribute a fixed percentage, such as 10%, of any month that comes in above baseline. Contributions are optional each month, which makes both plans a good fit for irregular income. Skipping retirement savings during lean years is common and understandable. Building it into the plan for above-baseline months, instead of treating it as an afterthought, makes it happen consistently. What's the Best Way to Handle Money During a Good Month? Extra money in a strong month should follow a set order, not a random spending decision. First, set aside the 25% to 30% tax portion described earlier. Second, refill the smoothing buffer if you drew from it during a recent slow month. Third, top off retirement contributions for months you skipped. Only after those three steps should extra income go toward discretionary spending or extra debt payoff. Writing this order down ahead of time removes the guesswork when a big check arrives. This order matters because taxes and buffer refills are due whether or not you feel like paying them. A good month that gets fully spent leaves nothing to cover the next slow one. Treating windfalls as scheduled tasks, not free money, keeps a variable-income budget working long term. How Do You Track Financial Progress When Income Isn't Steady? Track progress with net worth, not monthly income, since net worth smooths out the ups and downs of irregular pay. Net worth is what you own minus what you owe, checked on the same day each month or quarter. A slow month that still grows your net worth is a sign your system is working. ModernWallet's guide to calculating net worth walks through the full formula step by step. Update the same accounts each time — checking, savings, retirement, and debts — so the comparison stays accurate. Over a year, a rising trend line matters more than any single low month. Checking net worth quarterly, rather than daily, avoids the stress of watching balances jump around week to week. Irregular income naturally causes weekly noise. A quarterly view shows the real trend without that noise. Frequently asked questions How much of my freelance income should I set aside for taxes? Set aside 25% to 30% of every payment for federal income tax and self-employment tax combined. The exact percentage depends on your tax bracket, state taxes, and deductions, so check it against last year's actual tax bill. Move the money to a separate account right away, before it gets mixed in with spending cash. Should I budget based on my average income or my lowest month? Budget based on your lowest realistic month, not your average. An average hides the months you fall short, while a baseline built on your lowest month covers your bills every time. Treat income above that baseline as extra, to be assigned to taxes, buffer savings, and retirement. How big should an emergency fund be with irregular income? Plan for two separate amounts, not one flat number. A smoothing buffer covers the routine gap between your average and lowest months, refilled after every strong month. A true emergency reserve, for total loss of work, should hold three to six months of your baseline expenses. Do I still need to pay estimated taxes if a client withholds nothing? Yes, if you expect to owe $1,000 or more for the year, the IRS requires quarterly estimated payments. This applies to freelance, gig, and contract income, since no employer withholds tax on your behalf. Missing these payments can trigger a penalty even if you pay in full at filing time. What happens if I miss a quarterly estimated tax payment? The IRS can charge an underpayment penalty, calculated separately for each missed or late quarter. Paying late in one quarter and catching up later still reduces, but does not eliminate, the penalty for that quarter. Paying at least 90% of this year's tax, or 100% of last year's, generally avoids the penalty altogether. Can I contribute to a retirement account without an employer 401(k)? Yes, a SEP-IRA or a solo 401(k) both let self-employed workers save for retirement without an employer plan. Both are opened through a regular brokerage, not through a job, and both allow contributions based on a percentage of net self-employment earnings. Contributions are optional each year, which suits income that changes month to month. How often should I update my baseline income number? Recalculate your baseline every six to twelve months, or right after a major change in your client base. Adding or losing a large recurring client can shift your realistic low month significantly. Using outdated numbers means budgeting for income you no longer have, or missing income you could safely count on.
